feedback.text: Good structure and coverage, but it doesn't sound like us yet. The '30-60 minutes' and '12% fewer staff' figures have no source: frame them clearly as hypothetical examples or cut them. Rewrite the FAQ questions from the reader's side - Routematic speaks to the reader as 'you', not 'we/our'. Rename 'Conclusion: a practical monsoon playbook' to a short keyword-led heading. Too many one-line paragraphs; merge them into fuller 2-3 sentence paragraphs.

selectedWeaknesses.issue: Lack of explicit sourcing for specific figures and claims.
selectedWeaknesses.evidence: Scenario: a missed morning run leads to 12% fewer staff at the 10:00 slot, forcing overtime for other teams and impacting client SLAs the same day.
selectedWeaknesses.recommendation: Either frame specific figures and claims as hypothetical examples (e.g., 'for example, a 12% reduction...') or provide a source, clearly labeling internal data as such.
selectedWeaknesses.target: Operational impact on services, How quickly can dynamic rerouting be put in place for our existing fleet?

selectedWeaknesses.issue: Measured uses of 'we' per 1,000 words: 4.0 (routematic range 0–2.6)
selectedWeaknesses.recommendation: Use 'we' less; refer to the company in the third person.

selectedWeaknesses.issue: Measured bold phrases per 1,000 words: 22 (routematic range 2.8–17.4)
Measured share of one-sentence paragraphs: 0.71 (routematic range 0.104–0.574)
selectedWeaknesses.recommendation: Develop more paragraphs beyond one sentence.

instructions.instruction: Either frame the specific figures (the “30–60 minutes” and the “12% fewer staff”) clearly as hypothetical examples (prefix with “for example/eg.” and label as a hypothetical/example) OR remove them if you cannot provide a source. If you have internal data to support them, add a one-line note immediately after the figure: “(internal data).”
instructions.acceptanceCheck: Every occurrence of “30–60 minutes” or “12%” in the draft is either (a) prefixed with “for example” or similar and labeled as a hypothetical/example, or (b) removed, or (c) followed by “(internal data).” No unsupported statement of these exact figures remains without one of those treatments.

instructions.instruction: Reduce first-person plural usage: replace instances of “we/our/us” with “Routematic,” “you/your,” or neutral phrasing. Limit any remaining uses of “we/our/us” to no more than 2 occurrences per 1,000 words.
instructions.acceptanceCheck: A search shows no more than 2 occurrences of “we”/“our”/“us” per 1,000 words; company references in headings and lead sentences use “Routematic” rather than “we.”

instructions.instruction: Rewrite the intro and the opening sentence of each H2 to adopt Routematic’s practical, operational voice: remove promotional or marketing phrasing, focus on a concrete operational problem, and open the intro with a specific operational problem statement (e.g., describe the immediate operational impact of monsoon conditions).
instructions.acceptanceCheck: The intro’s first sentence names a specific operational problem and at least two H2 opening sentences read as practical, operational guidance rather than promotional language (no phrases like “industry‑leading” or similar).

instructions.instruction: Merge one-line paragraphs into fuller 2–3 sentence paragraphs so prose flows; keep single-sentence lines only for headings, captions, or list bullets.
instructions.acceptanceCheck: No standalone paragraph of exactly one sentence remains except in headings, captions, or bullets.

instructions.instruction: Rewrite every FAQ question so it speaks from the reader’s perspective (start with “How do I…”, “What should my team do when…”, “Can I…”, or use “you/your”), and remove any use of “we/our” from the question lines.
instructions.acceptanceCheck: All FAQ question lines address the reader (contain “you/your” or are phrased as “How do I…/What should I…/Can I…”) and contain no instances of “we” or “our.”

instructions.instruction: Replace the H2 “Conclusion: a practical monsoon playbook” with a short, keyword-led heading of 2–4 words (for example: “Monsoon playbook” or “Monsoon transport”).
instructions.acceptanceCheck: The H2 has been replaced and is 2–4 words long and includes either “monsoon” or “playbook.”

instructions.instruction: Remove inline bolding of phrases inside paragraph text; retain bold only for H2 headings (if needed).
instructions.acceptanceCheck: There is no bold formatting inside paragraph sentences; bold appears (if at all) only on H2 headings.

verification.evidence: add 30–60 minutes (hypothetical example) to routes. A single waterlogged stretch can cause whole shuttle runs to be cancelled, increasing payroll costs from paid but idle hours; reduce headcount available for morning shifts, affecting service delivery in BPO/GCC sites; and raise safety and legal exposure when employees, especially women or night-shift staff, are forced to wait at unsheltered pickup points. Scenario: a missed morning run leads to, for example, 12% fewer staff (hypothetical example) at the 10:00 slot, forcing overtime for other teams and impacting client SLAs the same day.
The revised draft contains 0 instances of "we", "our", or "us" per 1,000 words. The company reference in the lead sentence of the intro is "Routematic".

When heavy rain turns main roads into waterlogged bottlenecks, shuttles stop, employees miss shifts and your operations and payroll costs spike. That single morning closure can cascade into lost productive hours, missed SLAs and an anxious workforce — especially in cities where low-lying stretches and clogged drains are common. This article gives a practical, operational playbook — dynamic rerouting, communicating delays, safety rules for women and night-shift staff, and business continuity with transport vendors — so you can keep commutes running during monsoon flooding.
The revised draft contains no standalone paragraphs of exactly one sentence, except in headings, captions, or bullets.

How quickly can I put dynamic rerouting in place for my existing fleet? What is the minimum set of messages you should send to employees during heavy rain? What safety measures should your team make mandatory for night-shift pickups during the monsoon? What contract clauses protect your company if a vendor fails during prolonged flooding? How do I measure whether my monsoon plan actually reduced absenteeism?
The revised draft contains no bold formatting inside paragraph sentences; bold appears (if at all) only on H2 headings.
